newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. intends soon to pay $660 million to U.N.
newsitem.headline: U.S. intends soon to pay $660 million to U.N.

text.p: The United States intends to pay more than $660 million to the United Nations in the forthcoming months that would bring its 1996 dues up to date and make a dent in its debt for peacekeeping ventures, U.S. officials said on Friday.

With the world body nearly bankrupt because of the $1.6 billion U.S. debt, nearly every country speaking in the General Assembly, especially wealthy allies who foot most of the U.N. bills, have openly criticised the United States as a deadbeat for the past two years.
President Bill Clinton late on Monday signed an omnibus spending bill that provides funds for the United Nations and other international organisations.
The bill included $329 million for the U.N. regular budget for 1996 and for the Yugoslav war crimes tribunal, which is expected to be paid by the end of January.
In addition, Congress approved $282.4 million for current peacekeeping operations and another $50 million for peacekeeping arrears.

Before the monies can be paid, the State Department has to certify that the United Nations kept its zero growth budget and that its inspector general's office was still functioning. But a senior U.S. official said there would be no problem in both areas.

While the funds are more than the United Nations expected, they still leave a debt of about $750 million which will grow to about $1.4 billion at the beginning of 1997 when new assessments for member states are made.
Much of the monies owed are for peacekeeping ventures in past years, such as in Bosnia, which means some countries who contributed troops will not be paid for another year.

Washington, the largest payer in the United Nations, is assessed at 25 percent of the regular budget and more than 30 percent for peacekeeping. But Congress in September unilaterally lowered the peacekeeping contribution to 25 percent.

The United States has been behind in its payments for the past 10 years, skipping one year entirely. But with peacekeeping having multiplied in the early 1990s, reaching its peak two years ago at 70,000 troops, the debt became more visible. Peacekeeping in 1996 was greatly reduced after the United Nations' military role in Bosnia ended a year ago, with only 25,000 troops remaining.

U.N. officials are also annoyed that U.S. businessmen and the Pentagon have insisted on prompt payment for supplies sold to the United Nations, estimated at about $750 million annualy and much of it for peacekeeping. This income is in addition to the $2 billion New York City believes it earns by having the U.N. headquarters located there.
One difficulty in determining precisely who pays what to the United Nations is the world body's decentralized structure, once preferred by Washington but now a handicap to efficient management.

Edward Luck, senior policy adviser of the United Nations Association of the USA, a private research group, says that the regular U.N. budget covers only about a fifth of the staff costs, with voluntary and other contributions for specialised agencies and programmes exceeding those that are legally binding.
These agencies include the Vienna-based International Atomic Energy Agency and the Montreal-based International Civil Aviation Organisation.
